turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll just check your blood pressure before the doctor calls you. Pop your sleeve up for me.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. Sorry we're late, the car park was a joke, and the dog would not get in the boot, daft spaniel.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She means the dog, not me. I'm Dave, her husband.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Ha. Arm nice and relaxed. That's one hundred and forty eight over ninety two, pulse seventy eight.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that awful? I always go a bit funny in clinics. White coat thing, except you're not even wearing one.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): I'll leave the numbers with the doctor. Have a seat, he won't be a minute.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Come through. What can I do for you?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): It's my hands, doctor. They go dead in the night. The thumb, the index and the middle finger, both hands, right worse than the left, and I have to shake them to sort of wake them up.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. How long's that been happening?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Umm. Five-ish months? I couldn't tell you the day it started, it just crept in. And I keep dropping cups, which is mortifying, tea all over the packing bench.
[SEG0011] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two mugs this month, actually. I thought she was just tired.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Is the hand painful, or is it the numbness?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. Not painful. It's numb and tingly, like it's gone to sleep.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any of that numbness in the feet?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Never.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about neck pain, or pain shooting down from the neck?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neck's alright.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): The chairs on the line are a disgrace though, and they've shut the canteen, so everyone moans. That's not why I'm here.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mm. Does the grip go, apart from the cups? Any weakness?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Cups, and jars. Buttons are fiddly first thing. It eases if I shake the hand or hang it over the side of the bed.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mainly at night, or in the day as well?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Mainly nights, and when I first wake. If I'm driving and I grip the wheel a long time it comes on a bit. Oh, and the A38 was solid this morning, roadworks by the retail park, that's the other reason we were late.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ok. Any other medical problems?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): High blood pressure. I've been on tablets for years for that.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so the high blood pressure is still ongoing. Which tablet are you on now?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Err, the amlodopine, five milligrams, every morning. Before that it was ramipril, twenty milligram, and the GP swapped me off it about a year back.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She does take it. I've seen the box. Mostly.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I do take it, Dave. Don't start, not in front of the doctor.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): With the blood pressure, any headaches?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Well, sometimes, across the back of the head if a shift runs long.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain, or tightness in the chest?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that either.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swollen ankles?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): Family history. Anyone with hand trouble like this, or diabetes, heart disease?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Hand trouble, no. My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my sister's got the pressure but no sugar, and my brother had a heart attack at sixty. We skate round it at Sunday lunch, which is just as well, last week the yorkshires were like bricks.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): And work, food, exercise, alcohol, just so I've got the picture?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I work in the packing hall at the biscuit factory, twelve hour shifts, four on three off. Diet's whatever's going, sandwiches and crisps mostly. I don't exercise, not really, and I'll have a couple of pints on a Friday after the shift. That's my lot.

[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look at your hands, squeeze my fingers. Sensation is a bit dull over the thumb, index and middle finger on the right, and tapping the wrist sets the tingling off, that's Tinel's. No wasting in the thumb muscle. Now bend the wrists for Phalen's, and you've gone numb already.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's exactly it. Horrible.

[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): So, thinking aloud, this fits carpal tunnel, the median nerve getting pinched in the wrist, worse at night when the wrist curls. I can't completely rule out a nerve from the neck, but your neck's been fine and the pattern is very wrist.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Am I heading for an operation? Next door had his done and he was off driving for ages, and we do the grandson's school run Tuesdays. Uh, long story, my daughter and a broken-down Fiesta.

[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not surgery today. I'd like you to get a neutral wrist splint from the chemist and wear it at night, both wrists, for the next six weeks. Keep the wrist straight, don't sleep on a curled hand.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Both? The left one is milder, it only really plays up some nights.

[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): The left as well if it wakes you. If it hasn't settled in six weeks, we might send you for nerve conduction tests, to see how well the nerve is conducting. I'm not booking that now.
[SEG0046] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That blood pressure, one hundred and forty eight, is that ok if she's on the tablet?
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): It's a touch high for a single reading, and you were rushing. I'm not changing the amlodopine. Keep on the five milligrams every morning.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Do I wear the splint on the line? It moves quick, and a splint might catch on the boxes.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nights are the main thing. In the day, only if you're gripping a lot and you can take it off easily. Come back and see me in six weeks either way and we'll see how the hands are.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. I'll try and keep the tea in the cup till then. Err, the dog's in the car actually, windows cracked, he'll be fine.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll nag her about the splints. Shifts make her forgetful.
[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Ask reception to book that six week review on the way out.

spec.situation: Middle-aged office or factory worker with night-time numbness in thumb, index and middle fingers, shakes hands to wake them; dropping cups; splint advice, nerve test conditional.

traps.happens: The patient denies some symptoms (said as 'no', 'not really', 'never'), has a chronic condition named earlier (for example asthma or hypertension) and later the doctor asks about another symptom of it, and one answer is a double negative or a correction ('not that either', 'no... well, sometimes').
traps.label_rule: Denials go in negative_findings with the exact thing denied, never in symptoms. NEVER write a negative about a condition the patient has said they have. A corrected answer keeps only the final version. A negative is never a symptom, and 'not painful' is the finding 'pain' absent, not a symptom called 'painless'.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty=uncertain; symptom presence is stated clearly.
bad.text: Nocturnal finger numbness (category=neurological, status=present, duration=approximately 5 months, frequency=at night, onset=crept in, exact start date unknown, temporality=current, body_site=bilateral thumb, index and middle fingers, right worse than left, relieving_factors=shaking the hands, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Left wrist only if it wakes her; not unequivocally both wrists for six weeks.
bad.text: Wear a neutral wrist splint from the chemist at night on both wrists for six weeks, keeping the wrist straight and not sleeping on a curled hand, and in the daytime only if gripping a lot and it can be taken off easily (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient, time_reference=value: for the next six weeks)

omissions.text: Hand symptoms are described as numb and tingly 'like it's gone to sleep', not painful.
Hand symptoms are worse mainly at night and on first waking, and can also come on when driving/gripping the steering wheel for a long time.
Hanging the hand over the side of the bed relieves the symptoms.
The left hand is milder and only really plays up some nights.
No family history of similar hand trouble.
The discontinued ramipril was stopped about a year ago when the GP changed it.
Headache recording is misleading: patient denied headaches initially, then said only sometimes across the back of the head if a shift runs long.
Doctor said surgery is not planned now ('Not surgery today').
Doctor specifically said he is not booking nerve conduction tests now.
Patient was told to ask reception to book the six-week review on the way out.
